Advanced Earth Observation for Grassland Management
Improving Automated Mowing Detection Using Multimodal Remote Sensing and Machine Learning

Florian Klaver (July 2, 2026). Advanced Earth Observation for Grassland Management: Improving Automated Mowing Detection Using Multimodal Remote Sensing and Machine Learning. Keywords: mowing detection, Sentinel-2, Sentinel-1, interferometric coherence, SAR, machine learning, remote sensing, grassland management, change detection, Zurich Airport


Abstract
Satellite-based remote sensing provides a scalable approach to monitoring vegetation management across large areas. Automated detection of mowing events is relevant for grassland management applications, including airfield safety, where reliable mowing records support ecological monitoring. Preceding project work demonstrated that pixel-based machine learning models using Sentinel-2 optical imagery can detect mowing events, but identified two key limitations: dependence on cloud-free acquisitions and spatially fragmented predictions at the pixel level.
This thesis investigates two methodological extensions to address these limitations. First, Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data from the Sentinel-1 mission were integrated as a complementary data source. Both Ground Range Detected (GRD) backscatter and interferometric coherence derived from Single Look Complex (SLC) products were evaluated. Second, spatial postprocessing methods, including morphological filtering, median filtering, and superpixel-based aggregation, were implemented to reduce classification noise. An improved machine learning workflow incorporating refined feature selection, scene-level threshold calibration, and systematic model benchmarking was developed and evaluated against the preceding baseline. The study area is located at Zurich Airport, with ground truth mowing records spanning 2019 to 2023.
The results show that Sentinel-2 optical features remain the dominant predictors of mowing events. The best optical model achieved a test-set F1-Score of 0.923. GRD backscatter features provided no measurable improvement, achieving near-random performance in isolation. On parcel-level interferometric coherence showed a physically meaningful but weak and season-dependent signal: a statistically significant increase in VH coherence after mowing was observed only during the late growing season, while both polarisations showed negligible or inverted responses during the early and peak seasons. Coherence-only models performed near random at the pixel level, though selective fusion with optical features produced the highest test-set F1-Score within the coherence-eligible subset (0.922). At the operational scene level, the best models achieved F1-Scores of 0.689 and 0.749 on two held-out scenes, nearly doubling the performance of the preceding baseline (0.597 and 0.397 respectively). Scene-level threshold calibration emerged as the single most impactful operational improvement, substantially reducing false positives. Spatial postprocessing contributed only marginal additional gains, as threshold calibration had already addressed the dominant source of classification noise. A standalone prototype notebook was developed and applied to an external site near Lindau, where the model correctly identified known mowing events (recall = 0.997) and avoided false detections on non-grassland surfaces without requiring a land cover mask.
The findings indicate that optical vegetation indices, combined with appropriate threshold calibration and postprocessing, provide a robust basis for automated mowing detection. SAR interferometric coherence offers limited added value for pixel-based classification at this site, though parcel-level or segment-based approaches may yield better results. The primary bottleneck for further development remains the availability of spatially precise and diverse ground truth data.


Zusammenfassung
Satellitengestützte Fernerkundung bietet einen skalierbaren Ansatz zur Überwachung der Vegetationsbewirtschaftung über grosse Flächen. Die automatisierte Erkennung von Mähereignissen ist für verschiedene Anwendungen im Grünlandmanagement relevant, darunter die Flugsicherheit, wo zuverlässige Mähprotokolle das ökologische Monitoring unterstützen. Eine vorangegangene Projektarbeit zeigte, dass pixelbasierte Machine-Learning-Modelle mit optischen Sentinel-2-Daten Mähereignisse erkennen können, identifizierte jedoch zwei wesentliche Einschränkungen: die Abhängigkeit von wolkenfreien Aufnahmen und räumlich fragmentierte Vorhersagen auf Pixelebene.
Diese Bachelorarbeit untersucht zwei methodische Erweiterungen zur Behebung dieser Einschränkungen. Erstens wurden Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR)-Daten der Sentinel-1-Mission als komplementäre Datenquelle integriert. Sowohl Ground Range Detected (GRD)-Rückstreuung als auch interferometrische Kohärenz aus Single Look Complex (SLC)-Produkten wurden evaluiert. Zweitens wurden räumliche Post-Processing-Methoden, darunter morphologische Filterung, Medianfilterung und Superpixel-basierte Aggregation, zur Reduktion des Klassifikationsrauschens implementiert. Ein verbesserter Machine-Learning-Workflow mit optimierter Feature-Selektion, szenenbasierter Schwellwertkalibrierung und systematischem Modellvergleich wurde entwickelt und gegen die bestehende Baseline evaluiert. Das Untersuchungsgebiet liegt am Flughafen Zürich, mit Ground-Truth-Mähprotokollen aus den Jahren 2019 bis 2023.
Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass optische Sentinel-2-Features die dominanten Prädiktoren für Mähereignisse bleiben. Das beste optische Modell erreichte einen F1-Score von 0.923 auf dem Testdatensatz. GRD-Rückstreuungsfeatures lieferten keine messbare Verbesserung und erzielten isoliert nahezu zufällige Klassifikationsleistung. Auf Parzellenebene zeigte die interferometrische Kohärenz ein physikalisch plausibles, aber schwaches und saisonabhängiges Signal: ein statistisch signifikanter Anstieg der VH-Kohärenz nach dem Mähen wurde ausschliesslich in der späten Vegetationsperiode beobachtet, während beide Polarisationen in der frühen und mittleren Saison vernachlässigbare oder invertierte Reaktionen zeigten. Kohärenz-only Modelle erzielten auf Pixel-Level nahezu zufällig Ergebnisse, wobei die selektive Integration mit optischen Features den höchsten F1-Score innerhalb der kohärenzfähigen Teil-Gruppe ergab (0.922). Auf operationeller Szenenebene erreichten die besten Modelle F1-Scores von 0.689 und 0.749 auf zwei zurückgehaltenen Szenen, was die Leistung der vorangegangenen Baseline annähernd verdoppelte (0.597 bzw. 0.397). Die szenenbasierte Schwellwertkalibrierung erwies sich als die wirksamste operationelle Verbesserung und reduzierte falsch-positive Vorhersagen erheblich. Räumliches Post-Processing lieferte nur marginale zusätzliche Verbesserungen, da die Schwellwertkalibrierung die dominante Quelle des Klassifikationsrauschens bereits adressiert hatte. Ein eigenständiger Prototyp in Form eines interaktiven Jupyter Notebooks wurde entwickelt und auf ein externes Gebiet bei Lindau angewandt, wo das Modell bekannte Mähereignisse korrekt identifizierte (Recall = 0.997) und ohne Landbedeckungsmaske keine Fehldetektionen auf Nicht-Grünlandflächen produzierte.
Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass optische Vegetationsindizes in Kombination mit geeigneter Schwellwertkalibrierung und Post-Processing eine robuste Grundlage für die automatisierte Mäherkennung bieten. Interferometrische SAR-Kohärenz bietet auf dieser Untersuchungsfläche einen begrenzten Mehrwert für die pixelbasierte Klassifikation, wobei parzellenbasierte oder segmentbasierte Ansätze bessere Ergebnisse liefern könnten. Der wichtigste limitierende Faktor für die Weiterentwicklung bleibt die Verfügbarkeit von räumlich präzisen und diversen Ground-Truth-Daten.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1  Introduction



Grassland management at airports is a safety-critical task. Vegetation height and structure on airfield grounds directly influence habitat attractiveness for bird species, which in turn affects the frequency and severity of bird strikes (DeVault et al. 2011). At Zurich Airport, grasslands are subject to regular mowing protocols designed to reduce wildlife hazards. However, monitoring when and where mowing occurs has traditionally relied on manual records created by field staff, a process that is labour-intensive and prone to spatial inaccuracies. The quality and completeness of these records also directly constrain the training and validation of any supervised classification model built on them. To develop a reliable automated detection system, both the remote sensing methodology and the underlying reference data must be addressed.
Satellite-based remote sensing offers a scalable alternative to manual monitoring. The Sentinel-2 constellation, operated by the European Space Agency, provides multispectral imagery at 10 to 20 metre spatial resolution with a revisit cycle of approximately five days (Drusch et al. 2012). Vegetation indices derived from these data, such as the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and the Normalized Difference Infrared Index (NDII), capture the spectral response of vegetation to management events like mowing, where the abrupt removal of biomass produces a measurable drop in reflectance values (Pettorelli et al. 2005; Andreatta et al. 2022).
In previous project work, a pixel-based machine learning workflow for automated mowing detection at Zurich Airport using Sentinel-2 imagery was developed (Klaver 2025). That study demonstrated that standard classifiers, particularly the Support Vector Machine, can detect mowing events with high accuracy on controlled test samples (F1-Score of 0.923). However, the work also identified two fundamental limitations that prevent the system from functioning as a reliable operational tool.
The first limitation concerns data availability. Optical sensors depend on clear atmospheric conditions, and in the temperate climate of central Switzerland, frequent cloud cover creates gaps in the time series that can prevent the acquisition of usable pre- and post-event image pairs required for change detection. This problem is well documented in the literature. De Vroey et al. (2021) highlight that relying solely on optical data is particularly problematic in regions where cloud cover is persistent during the growing season. Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), which operates independently of weather and illumination conditions, has been proposed as a complementary data source. Several studies have demonstrated that interferometric coherence derived from SAR acquisitions can detect vegetation changes such as mowing, because the removal of biomass alters the scattering properties of the surface (Tamm et al. 2016; Zalite et al. 2016; Reinermann et al. 2022).
The second limitation concerns spatial consistency. The pixel-based classification approach produces predictions independently for each pixel, resulting in spatially fragmented output with characteristic salt-and-pepper noise (Blaschke 2010). In the full-scene application conducted in the previous study, models that performed well on test metrics produced scattered false positives across the scene and failed to reconstruct the contiguous shapes of mowing events (Klaver 2025). Spatial postprocessing techniques, such as morphological filtering (Jamil et al. 2008) and superpixel-based segmentation (Achanta et al. 2012), can address this issue by incorporating neighbourhood context into the classification output. These methods have been applied in remote sensing contexts to improve the spatial coherence of pixel-based classifications (Dharani and Sreenivasulu 2021; Crommelinck et al. 2017), though their specific application to mowing detection remains underexplored.
Based on the limitations identified in the previous study, this thesis addresses the following research questions:

Can the integration of Sentinel-1 SAR data improve mowing detection performance compared to a purely optical approach, and reduce the workflow’s dependence on cloud-free acquisitions?
To what extent do spatial postprocessing methods such as morphological filtering and superpixel-based segmentation improve the spatial consistency of pixel-based classification outputs?
Can the availability and quality of ground truth data for mowing detection be improved through acquisition of additional reference datasets beyond the existing airport records?
How does the enhanced workflow compare to the baseline model from the previous study in terms of detection accuracy and operational reliability?

title: 2  Literature Review
text:
2.1 Optical Remote Sensing for Grassland Monitoring
This chapter reviews the theoretical foundations relevant to the two main methodological extensions introduced in this thesis: the integration of Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data and the application of spatial postprocessing techniques. Optical remote sensing with Sentinel-2, vegetation index theory, and the pixel-based machine learning workflow that serves as the baseline for this work are kept brief here, for a detailed treatment please refer to the preceding project work (Klaver 2025).
Satellite-based optical remote sensing enables continuous observation of vegetation dynamics across large spatial and temporal scales. The Sentinel-2 mission provides multispectral imagery in 13 spectral bands spanning visible, near-infrared, and short-wave infrared wavelengths, with spatial resolutions between 10 and 60 metres and a revisit cycle of approximately five days (Drusch et al. 2012). Vegetation indices derived from these bands quantify biophysical properties of vegetation. The Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), which exploits the contrast between red absorption and near-infrared reflectance, is the most widely used indicator of vegetation health and biomass (Pettorelli et al. 2005). The Normalized Difference Infrared Index (NDII), which incorporates the short-wave infrared band sensitive to leaf water content, has been shown to yield high accuracy for mowing frequency detection, in some cases outperforming NDVI-based approaches (Andreatta et al. 2022). Both indices respond to the abrupt removal of standing biomass during mowing, producing a sharp drop that can be distinguished from the gradual changes associated with phenological development.
Automated mowing detection from optical time series has been approached through both rule-based threshold methods and supervised machine learning classifiers (Reinermann et al. 2022; Garioud et al. 2019). Comparative work suggests that simpler models such as Random Forest and Support Vector Machines can match more complex approaches when training data is limited (Garioud et al. 2019), a finding directly relevant to operational settings where labelled reference data is scarce. For a broader overview of remote sensing approaches for grassland monitoring, see Reinermann et al. (2020).
Despite the effectiveness of optical approaches, their operational reliability is constrained by atmospheric conditions. In temperate climates, cloud cover frequently disrupts the temporal continuity of observations required for change detection (De Vroey et al. 2021). This limitation motivates the integration of weather-independent data sources such as SAR.

title: 2  Literature Review
text:
2.2 Synthetic Aperture Radar
Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) is an active microwave imaging technology. Unlike optical sensors, which passively record reflected sunlight, a SAR instrument transmits its own microwave pulses and records the backscattered signal. Because SAR operates at microwave wavelengths, it can penetrate cloud cover and acquire data independently of solar illumination while achieving high spatial resolution through aperture synthesis along the flight path (Meyer 2019).
A SAR sensor records both the amplitude and the phase of the returned signal. The amplitude depends on surface properties such as roughness, moisture content, and vegetation structure. The phase encodes the round-trip distance between sensor and surface and is essential for interferometric techniques discussed below. SAR systems can transmit and receive signals in different polarisation orientations, typically horizontal (H) or vertical (V). The notation describes the transmit-receive combination: VV (vertical transmit, vertical receive) measures co-polarised backscatter, primarily sensitive to surface roughness and soil structure, while VH (vertical transmit, horizontal receive) measures cross-polarised backscatter, arising predominantly from volume scattering within vegetation canopies (Meyer 2019). The cross-polarised channel is therefore particularly relevant for detecting vegetation structure changes such as mowing. The cross-ratio, defined as the difference VH minus VV in decibel scale, provides a normalised indicator that reduces the influence of viewing geometry on the measured signal. Because VV and VH respond similarly to changes in incidence angle but differently to vegetation structure, their difference isolates the vegetation signal from geometric effects.

2.2.1 The Sentinel-1 Mission
The Sentinel-1 mission operates a C-band SAR instrument at a wavelength of approximately 5.6 cm in dual polarisation mode (VV+VH). In its primary Interferometric Wide Swath (IW) mode, it achieves a spatial resolution of 5 by 20 metres with a 250 km swath width (ESA 2013). The mission distributes data in different product types: Level-1 Single Look Complex (SLC) products retain both amplitude and phase information, while Level-1 Ground Range Detected (GRD) products discard the phase during processing. This makes the GRD product simpler to access and process, but limits its utility for interferometric analysis (ESA 2013; Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem 2025).


2.2.2 Interferometric Coherence
When two SAR SLC acquisitions are taken from nearly the same orbital position at different times, their complex signals can be compared through a technique known as SAR interferometry (InSAR). The interferometric coherence quantifies the degree of similarity between the two complex signals and is expressed as a value between 0 and 1 (Tamm et al. 2016). Given two complex SAR images \(s_1\) and \(s_2\), the coherence \(\gamma\) is calculated as:
\[\gamma = \frac{|\langle s_1 s_2^* \rangle|}{\sqrt{\langle s_1 s_1^* \rangle \langle s_2 s_2^* \rangle}}, \quad 0 \leq \gamma \leq 1 \tag{2.1}\]
where \(|\cdot|\) denotes the absolute value, \(\langle \cdot \rangle\) denotes a spatial averaging operation and \(^*\) denotes the complex conjugate. A coherence value near 1 indicates that the position and scattering properties of the surface elements remained stable between the two acquisitions, while a value near 0 indicates complete decorrelation (Tamm et al. 2016).
For vegetated surfaces, temporal decorrelation is driven by continuous changes in canopy geometry through leaf movement, growth, and moisture fluctuations, which cause progressive phase decorrelation. When vegetation is removed through mowing, the exposed soil or short stubble presents a more stable scattering surface, leading to higher coherence. This mechanism makes interferometric coherence a potentially useful indicator for mowing detection.
The measured coherence is not solely determined by temporal change on the ground. Tamm et al. (2016) decompose the total estimated coherence as \(\gamma_{total} = \gamma_{temporal} \cdot \gamma_{SNR} \cdot \gamma_{bias} \cdot \gamma_{other}\), where \(\gamma_{temporal}\) captures physical surface changes and \(\gamma_{SNR}\) accounts for decorrelation due to system thermal noise, and the remaining terms capture processing-related and volumetric effects. For most applications the non-temporal terms are negligible, but the weak interaction between C-band radar and grassland vegetation produces lower signal-to-noise ratios, making SNR correction non-negligible for grassland monitoring (Tamm et al. 2016).
Tamm et al. (2016) investigated the coherence response to mowing using Sentinel-1 C-band data with 12-day temporal baselines. Both VH and VV polarisation coherence values were significantly higher after mowing, with the strongest increase occurring shortly after the event and elevated values persisting for up to 36 days. However, precipitation decreased coherence regardless of vegetation state, and rapid regrowth within the 12-day revisit period reduced the coherence contrast. Zalite et al. (2016) confirmed that interferometric coherence is sensitive to mowing using X-band SAR, though coherence responses may differ across wavelengths due to different vegetation penetration depths (Meyer 2019).


2.2.3 SAR-Optical Fusion for Mowing Detection
Several studies have combined SAR and optical data for mowing detection with mixed results. De Vroey et al. (2021) found that 54% of mowing events in hay meadows could be detected from Sentinel-1 coherence jumps, with grazing events identified as a major source of false detections. Reinermann et al. (2022) tested an integrated S1+S2 approach for Germany, where the optical-only method achieved an F1-Score of 0.64 but the combined approach reduced this to 0.61 due to increased false positives. Komisarenko et al. (2022) used a deep learning model with both S1 and S2 time series in Estonia, achieving an event accuracy of 73.3%. These findings highlight that SAR-optical fusion does not automatically improve performance and that careful integration strategies are necessary.

title: 2  Literature Review
text:
2.3 Spatial Postprocessing Methods
Pixel-based classification methods treat each pixel independently, without considering the spatial relationship between neighbouring predictions. This frequently produces fragmented classification outputs containing isolated misclassified pixels, commonly referred to as salt-and-pepper noise (Blaschke 2010). Object-Based Image Analysis (OBIA), which segments images into meaningful objects prior to classification, has been proposed as one paradigm to address this limitation (Blaschke 2010). However, OBIA requires fundamentally restructuring the classification workflow and assumes that the segmentation units correspond to areas of uniform class membership. For mowing detection, this assumption is problematic because mowing events frequently affect only parts of grassland parcels, meaning that any predefined object boundary risks misrepresenting the actual spatial extent of the event. An alternative is to retain the pixel-based approach and apply spatial postprocessing to the classification output. This preserves the simplicity of per-pixel classifiers while using spatial context to reduce noise after the fact. The following methods represent three such postprocessing strategies at different spatial scales.
A simple baseline approach is the median filter, which replaces each pixel’s class label with the most frequent label within a local neighbourhood window, suppressing isolated misclassifications while largely preserving edges (MathWorks 2026).
Mathematical morphology provides a more structured set of spatial operations for refining binary or categorical classification outputs. The two fundamental operations are erosion, which removes small isolated regions by shrinking object boundaries, and dilation, which expands regions and fills small gaps. Combinations of these are commonly used in practice: opening (erosion followed by dilation) removes small spurious objects, while closing (dilation followed by erosion) fills small holes and smooths boundaries (Jamil et al. 2008). These operations have been applied in remote sensing classification workflows to reduce isolated false detections while preserving the broader structure of larger classified regions (Dharani and Sreenivasulu 2021). For mowing detection, where events are expected to affect spatially contiguous areas within grassland parcels rather than isolated single pixels, morphological postprocessing can bring pixel-level predictions closer to the expected spatial scale of the target phenomenon.
An alternative approach to spatial regularisation is superpixel segmentation, which groups neighbouring pixels into compact, spectrally homogeneous clusters. The Simple Linear Iterative Clustering (SLIC) algorithm is one of the most widely used methods for this purpose. SLIC adapts k-means clustering to operate jointly in the spatial and spectral domain, producing approximately uniform segments efficiently with O(N) complexity (Achanta et al. 2012). The compactness and size of the resulting segments are controlled by two parameters: the number of desired superpixels and a compactness weight that balances spatial proximity against spectral similarity (Achanta et al. 2012). In geospatial applications, SLIC has been applied to high-resolution imagery for object delineation, where its segments have been shown to adhere well to natural image boundaries (Crommelinck et al. 2017). In a classification postprocessing context, pixel-level predictions can be aggregated within each superpixel segment through majority voting, assigning all pixels within a segment the dominant class label. This enforces local spatial consistency and reduces isolated misclassifications within otherwise homogeneous areas.

text:
3.1 Study Area and Data Sources
The study area comprises the perimeter of Zurich Airport (Flughafen Zürich). The airport grasslands are subject to regular mowing regimes designed to manage vegetation height and reduce wildlife hazard risk. Figure 3.1 illustrates the spatial extent of the study area, highlighting the airport boundary and the specific grassy areas within it that are relevant for mowing event detection. A detailed description of the study area and its operational context is provided in the preceding project work (Klaver 2025).
The analysis draws on five primary data sources, summarised in Table 3.1. Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery and the associated ground truth mowing records were carried over from the previous study (Klaver 2025). Sentinel-1 Single Ground Range Detected (GRD) and Look Complex (SLC) data were newly acquired for this thesis to add SAR features to the analysis. Grassland parcels from the official Swiss land survey (Amtliche Vermessung) were used to constrain the analysis to vegetated areas and exclude non-grassland areas such as forests, built-up surfaces, roads, and runways.
The Sentinel-2 archive contains 201 cloud-masked scenes across the study period. No data were available for 2022 due to a gap in the local archive. The ground truth dataset consists of 1,899 mowing event polygons, recorded by farmers responsible for the mowing on maps and digitalised by project staff of the ZHAW. Each polygon is attributed with a mowing date. These records were cleaned by intersecting them with the grassland class from the Swiss land survey and removing fragments smaller than 400 m², resulting in 3,008 polygon fragments from 1,860 unique mowing events (Klaver 2025).
At the beginning of this thesis, extensive efforts were made to acquire additional ground truth data from external institutions and research groups to expand the training and validation basis beyond the airport. However, no suitable datasets of sufficient size and with the required spatial and temporal resolution could be obtained. The analysis therefore relies mainly on the Zurich Airport ground truth for model training and evaluation. A small number of additional mowing records from Lindau (provided by Strickhof) and Aadorf (provided by Agroscope) were obtained for use in qualitative validation of the model’s generalisation performance outside the airport study area.

3.2 Sentinel-2 Preprocessing and Feature Engineering
The Sentinel-2 preprocessing and feature engineering workflow was carried over from the previous project work and is described in detail in Klaver (2025). This section summarises the key steps and parameters for completeness.
All 201 Sentinel-2 scenes were reprojected from EPSG:32632 (UTM Zone 32N) to EPSG:2056 (Swiss LV95) using bilinear resampling, producing a uniform reference grid of 559 by 381 pixels at 10 m resolution. This grid defines the spatial reference for all subsequent raster operations in the pipeline. Cloud masking was applied per pixel using the cloud probability band (band 13), setting all pixels with a probability exceeding 30% to NaN.
For each of the 227 ground truth mowing dates, the pipeline searches for a temporal triplet of three Sentinel-2 scenes in defined time windows relative to the event date, as shown in Table 3.2 and Figure 3.2. Events where all three images are available form a complete triplet. Of the 227 events, 92 produced valid triplets.

For each mowing event, three satellite acquisitions are identified: \(t_{n-2}\) (before far), \(t_{n-1}\) (before near), and \(t_{n+1}\) (after). The negative (not mowed) pair spans \(t_{n-2}\) to \(t_{n-1}\), a period without mowing. The positive (mowed) pair spans \(t_{n-1}\) to \(t_{n+1}\), capturing the vegetation change caused by the mowing event. \(t_n\) represents the mowing event date.



For each triplet, two feature sets are computed. The positive (mowed) pair uses the before near and after images, while the negative (not mowed) pair uses the before far and before near images. Five vegetation indices are calculated for each pair: NDVI, EVI, SAVI, GNDVI, and NDII. Together with their temporal differences and the corresponding raw band values and differences, this yields 20 features per pixel. The vegetation index formulas and their spectral basis are documented in Klaver (2025).
Training samples are drawn from within the ground truth polygons after applying a one-pixel (10 m) binary erosion to avoid edge effects at polygon boundaries. Sampling is balanced per event per class. After excluding events with insufficient valid pixels due to cloud cover, the final training dataset contains 33’368 samples from 63 unique mowing events.

title: 3  Methods
section: 3.3 SAR Data Acquisition and Coherence Estimation
text:
3.3 SAR Data Acquisition and Coherence Estimation

3.3.1 GRD Backscatter
As an initial approach, Sentinel-1 Ground Range Detected (GRD) images were acquired through Google Earth Engine for all training events. The GEE collection provided 471 ascending-orbit scenes in Interferometric Wide Swath (IW) mode with VV and VH polarisations over the study period. The images were speckle-filtered using a square spatial mean kernel with a 30 m radius, exported at 10 m resolution in EPSG:2056, and aligned to the Sentinel-2 reference grid. Six features were derived per event from the before near and after GRD images: the absolute VV, VH, and cross-ratio (VH minus VV) values of the after image, and the corresponding temporal differences.
However, preliminary experiments during the development phase indicated that GRD backscatter features did not provide sufficient discriminative power for mowing detection (see Section 4.3 for details). This motivated the transition to interferometric coherence derived from SLC products, which captures phase-level information not available in GRD data (Tamm et al. 2016).


3.3.2 SLC Acquisition
Single Look Complex (SLC) products were acquired from the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem (CDSE) (Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem 2025) using the cdsetool Python library (Vejby 2026). A metadata query for ascending IW SLC products over the study area between 2019 and 2023 returned 633 available scenes. From these, relative orbit 15 was selected as it provides the most consistent coverage over Zurich Airport (387 scenes). The IW2 subswath was identified as covering the study area for this orbit geometry.


3.3.3 Coherence Quadruplet Design
The coherence feature design requires a different temporal logic than the optical features. While vegetation indices capture the spectral state at a single point in time, interferometric coherence quantifies the phase stability between two SAR acquisitions. Tall, unmowed grass produces low coherence due to wind-induced movement, short stubble after mowing presents a stable surface with high coherence. Critically, a coherence pair spanning the mowing event itself would also yield low coherence, because the surface changed between acquisitions, making it indistinguishable from the unmowed case.
To resolve this, the coherence estimation uses four SLC acquisitions per mowing event rather than the three used for optical features (see Figure 3.3). For the negative (not mowed) class, coherence is computed between two pre-mowing acquisitions (\(t_{n-2}\) to \(t_{n-1}\)), both captured while the grass is tall and signal unstable. For the positive (mowed) class, coherence is computed between two post-mowing acquisitions (\(t_{n+1}\) to \(t_{n+2}\)), both captured after the grass has been cut and the signal is stable.






Figure 3.3: Coherence quadruplet design. Unlike the optical triplet (Figure 3.2), coherence estimation requires both acquisitions of each pair to fall on the same side of the mowing event.



The first three SLC dates are matched to the optical triplet dates within a tolerance of 8 days, while the fourth acquisition (\(t_{n+2}\)) is selected as the next same-orbit overpass exactly 6 or 12 days after \(t_{n+1}\). All temporal baselines within each coherence pair must equal 6 or 12 days, corresponding to the Sentinel-1 repeat cycle All acquisitions must originate from the same relative orbit and subswath to preserve the phase relationship. Of the 92 events with the full S2 temporal triplet, 72 produced valid SLC quadruplets. The remaining 20 events were excluded because they did not fulfil the strict temporal matching criteria.


3.3.4 SNAP Processing
Interferometric coherence was computed using ESA’s SNAP Graph Processing Tool (GPT), called from Python via subprocess in batch mode (ESA 2026a, 2026b). For each SLC pair, the processing chain applied subswath splitting (IW2, VV and VH), precise orbit correction, back-geocoding with the SRTM 3-arcsecond DEM, and coherence estimation using a 19 x 5 pixel averaging window following Tamm et al. (2016). The result was debursted and terrain-corrected to a 20 m output grid in EPSG:2056 using the SRTM 1-arcsecond DEM, producing a two-band GeoTIFF with VV and VH coherence values in [0, 1].
A subset of SLC pairs produced invalid coherence outputs all bands contained only zero values, despite SNAP reporting successful processing. The cause of these silent failures could not be identified nor fixed, and affected 36 of the 72 pairs. Affected events were detected by automated validation checks and excluded from further analysis, reducing the number of valid coherence pairs to 36. Manual inspection of affected outputs confirmed that all bands contained exclusively zero values despite correct input data, but no consistent pattern in acquisition date, orbit geometry, or temporal baseline could be identified as the cause.


3.3.5 SNR Decorrelation Correction
Following the approach described by Tamm et al. (2016), a post-hoc correction for signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) decorrelation was applied to all coherence rasters. The correction isolates the temporal decorrelation component by dividing the measured coherence by the estimated SNR decorrelation factor, \(\gamma_{SNR}\).
The SNR decorrelation factor for an interferometric pair was estimated using GRD backscatter images as a proxy for the radar cross-section \(\sigma^0\). For each SLC acquisition date, the nearest GRD image within 3 days was identified and resampled from the 10 m GRD grid to the 20 m coherence grid. The per-pixel SNR decorrelation was then computed following Equation 3 of Tamm et al. (2016): \[\gamma_{SNR} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\left(1 + \frac{1}{SNR_{t_1}}\right)\left(1 + \frac{1}{SNR_{t_2}}\right)}} \tag{3.1}\]
where \(SNR = (\sigma^0 - NESZ) / NESZ\) for each acquisition. The noise equivalent sigma zero (NESZ) was approximated as -25.0 dB for VV and -27.0 dB for VH polarisation. These values fall within the range of measured NESZ performance for the IW2 subswath, which is typically several decibels below the mission requirement specification of -22 dB reported in the system documentation (ESA 2013). Because per-pixel NESZ varies with incidence angle and burst position, these fixed approximations introduce some uncertainty into the correction, particularly for low-backscatter pixels near the noise floor. A minimum floor of \(\gamma_{SNR} = 0.10\) was applied to prevent excessive amplification in low-backscatter areas. The corrected coherence was obtained as \(\gamma_{corrected} = \gamma_{measured} / \gamma_{SNR}\), clipped to [0, 1].
To quantify the effect of both raw and SNR-corrected coherence on class separability, Cohen’s \(d\) effect sizes and Mann-Whitney p-values were computed between mowed and unmowed parcels on post-event coherence (coh_after) for each polarisation and seasonal window. This analysis compares coherence spatially across parcels: for a given event window, the post-event coherence of parcels where mowing was recorded is compared against parcels where no mowing occurred. The growing season was divided into three periods: early (April to May), peak (June to July), and late (August to October). Based on the quadruplet design described above, a positive Cohen’s \(d\) indicates that mowed parcels show higher post-event coherence than unmowed parcels. The results of this analysis are reported in Section 4.1.

title: 3  Methods
text:
3.4 Feature Fusion and Model Configurations
To combine features from different sensor sources, GRD and coherence values were attached to the existing Sentinel-2 training samples by sampling the corresponding rasters at the exact geographic coordinates of each pixel. For GRD features, which share the same 10 m grid as the Sentinel-2 data, this extraction is spatially exact. Coherence rasters, produced at 20 m resolution, were resampled to the 10 m grid using bilinear interpolation before sampling. Because the Sentinel-2 samples were filtered for cloud cover during the optical preprocessing stage, not all events with valid coherence rasters retained usable training pixels. Consequently, the dataset was divided into two distinct groups to accommodate the differing data availability. Group A comprises the full set of 63 events with valid Sentinel-2 and GRD data, yielding 33,368 samples. Group B consists of the restricted subset of 24 events that also possess valid interferometric coherence pairs and corresponding cloud-free Sentinel-2 samples, consisting of 15,311 samples.
The assignment of coherence values follows the quadruplet design described in Section 3.3. Positive samples (label = 1, mowed) receive coherence values from the post-mowing pair (\(t_{n+1}\) to \(t_{n+2}\)), representing short vegetation. Negative samples (label = 0, not mowed) receive coherence values from the pre-mowing pair (\(t_{n-2}\) to \(t_{n-1}\)), representing tall vegetation. Both VV and VH polarisation coherence values are included as features.
The data were split into training and test sets using GroupShuffleSplit with a test fraction of 0.2, grouped by event identifier (match_id). This ensures that all samples from a given mowing event appear exclusively in either the training or the test set, preventing data leakage between spatially and temporally correlated pixels. For Group A, this procedure produced a split of 50 training and 13 test events (24,945 and 8,423 samples respectively). For Group B, the split resulted in 19 training and 5 test events (12,023 and 3,288 samples).
Feature selection was performed exclusively on the training split to prevent test-set leakage. This step was conducted on both sample subsets A and B and the results compared to find the best feature sets. Compared to the preceding project work (Klaver 2025), which relied on simpler reduction, a more systematic feature importance analysis was conducted using three complementary methods: Pearson correlation analysis to identify redundant feature pairs (threshold \(∣r∣ > 0.85\)), Mean Decrease Impurity (MDI) from a preliminary Random Forest classifier to rank features by their contribution to node purity (Breiman 2001), and permutation importance to quantify each feature’s contribution to generalisation performance by measuring the decrease in F1-score after randomly shuffling that feature (Altmann et al. 2010). Features with permutation importance values near zero or below zero were mostly discarded, and among correlated pairs the feature with the lower importance was removed.
While these analytical methods identified several post-event (_after) features as highly informative, temporal difference features (_diff) are considered structurally more robust across different sites and conditions, as they capture relative change rather than absolute reflectance that varies with soil type, grass species, or geography. Consequently, the final model configurations balanced the analytical findings with domain expectations. The detailed outcomes are presented in Section 4.2.
Eight model configurations were defined across the two groups, as summarised in Table 3.3. Configurations within Group A utilise Sentinel-2 and GRD features exclusively. Configurations within Group B incorporate the coherence features alongside the optical and GRD data. Because the two groups utilise separate train-test splits, their respective performance metrics are not directly comparable.

3.5 Classification and Threshold Calibration
Following the same approach as in the previous study (Klaver 2025), three classifiers were trained for each of the eight model configurations: Support Vector Machine (SVM) (Cortes and Vapnik 1995), Random Forest (RF) (Breiman 2001), and Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LGBM) (Ke et al. 2017). All classifiers were implemented using scikit-learn compatible pipelines. The SVM pipeline includes a StandardScaler for feature normalisation prior to classification. The tree-based models (RF, LightGBM) operate on unscaled features.
Hyperparameter tuning was performed using GridSearchCV with GroupKFold cross-validation (5 folds), optimising for the F1-Score. The parameter grids are summarised in Table 3.4.

The default classification threshold of 0.5 on the predicted probability is calibrated for balanced class distributions. At real scene-level class balance, where often less than 10% of grassland pixels are mowed at any given time, this threshold produces excessive false positive predictions. To address this, a scene-level threshold calibration was performed using a leave-one-out (LOO) approach (scikit-learn developers 2026b) over six mostly cloud-free calibration scenes with available ground truth. For each calibration scene, the full feature set was computed and the model was applied across a threshold sweep from 0.10 to 0.95 in steps of 0.05. The threshold maximising the F1-Score was recorded per scene, and the final operational threshold was set as the median across all calibration scenes. This calibration was performed independently for each of the models that were actually applied on full scenes later. Certain models that performed poorly in training were not included in the scene-level evaluation and threshold calibration, as they were not considered for operational use. The final calibrated thresholds are reported in Section 4.4.

title: 3  Methods
text:
3.6 Spatial Postprocessing
Three spatial postprocessing methods were applied to the binary classification outputs to reduce salt-and-pepper noise and improve spatial consistency. The methods operate on the predicted mowing maps, where each pixel is encoded as mowed (1), not mowed (0), or nodata (-1).
The first method is a median filter with a configurable window size, which replaces isolated misclassified pixels with the majority label of their local surroundings. The second method applies morphological operations in sequence: binary opening (erosion followed by dilation) removes small spurious detections, followed by binary closing (dilation followed by erosion) to fill small gaps within classified regions. Both operations use a disk-shaped structuring element with a configurable radius. After the morphological operations, connected components smaller than a specified minimum area are removed. The third method uses SLIC superpixel segmentation to aggregate pixel-level predictions. The segmentation is computed from the spectral bands of the input scene and within each resulting segment, majority voting assigns all pixels the dominant class label.
The three methods can be chained in sequence. To determine the optimal postprocessing configuration, a grid search was performed over the parameter space defined in Table 3.5. Each configuration was evaluated on the six calibration scenes used for threshold calibration, and the configuration maximising the mean F1-Score across all scenes was selected as the operational postprocessing setting. The grid search was conducted using the most stable model from the scene-level evaluation before postprocessing (S2_only_diff SVM) with its calibrated threshold. The resulting best configuration and its effect on classification performance are reported in Section 4.5.

title: 3  Methods
text:
3.7 Evaluation
Model performance was assessed at two levels. On the training data, pixel-level classification performance was evaluated using standard metrics, specifically accuracy, precision, recall, the F1-Score, and the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (ROC AUC) (scikit-learn developers 2026a). Additionally, confusion matrices were generated to visualize the balance between false positive and false negative predictions. These metrics were computed for each model configuration using the held-out test events from the GroupShuffleSplit.
Pixel-based metrics on sampled training data can overestimate true operational performance in geospatial domains (Meyer et al. 2019; Ploton et al. 2020). Therefore, based on test-set performance across all 24 trained models, 11 were selected for scene-level evaluation. The selection prioritised the best-performing SVM and RF variants across the feature configurations, while excluding LightGBM models, which consistently underperformed in this and the preceding study. Since multiple mowing events can occur within the temporal window spanned by a scene pair, a composite ground truth mask was constructed for each evaluation scene. This mask distinguishes between definite mowing pixels, where the ground truth unambiguously indicates mowing within the scene pair interval, and boundary pixels, where the temporal assignment is ambiguous due to overlapping or adjacent events (e.g., event occuring at the same date as the before- or after-image of the chosen scene). Such boundary pixels were excluded from both the positive and negative class during scoring to avoid penalising the model for predictions in temporally uncertain areas. Pixel-level accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-Score for the mowed class were computed on the remaining definite and non-mowed pixels. Each model was evaluated on two mostly cloud-free composite scenes using its LOO-calibrated threshold, both with and without the best postprocessing configuration determined by the grid search described in Section 3.6. Spatial difference maps showing true positives, false positives, false negatives, and boundary detections overlaid on the Sentinel-2 RGB composite were generated to support qualitative assessment of prediction patterns and error sources.
To directly quantify the improvement over the preceding study, the best-performing model from PW2 (SVM trained on ndii_diff as the sole feature) was applied to the same two evaluation scenes using its original default threshold of 0.5 and without postprocessing. This allows a fair comparison between the previous and current workflow under identical scene conditions.
In addition to the standard evaluation on mowing scenes, a control test was conducted to assess the model’s false positive behaviour in the absence of mowing. For a selected event, the S2_only_diff SVM model was applied to the before-far (\(t_{n-2}\)) to before-near (\(t_{n-1}\)) image pair rather than the before-near to after pair. In this time window, no mowing is expected to have occurred on the areas identified as mowed in the ground truth for the true event period. The control test measures the proportion of ground truth mowed pixels that the model incorrectly predicts as mowed during this non-mowing period. A low false positive rate in the control window provides additional confidence that the model responds to actual mowing signals rather than to unrelated spectral or coherence variations.

title: 3  Methods
text:
3.8 Operational Prototype and Generalisation Test
To support practical application of the developed methodology, a standalone prototype was produced as an interactive Jupyter Notebook. The tool is designed for end-users such as environmental researchers or land managers, allowing them to apply the mowing detection workflow without requiring the full training pipeline or dependencies on the project’s source code. The user provides two Sentinel-2 GeoTIFFs (a before and after image bracketing the suspected mowing event), loads a pre-trained model file, and optionally supplies a study area boundary, grassland mask, or ground truth polygons for evaluation. The notebook then handles feature computation, cloud masking, model prediction, and postprocessing automatically. Only the S2-only model configurations are included, as the acquisition and preprocessing complexity of interferometric coherence estimation would undermine the tool’s purpose as a lightweight, accessible application.
To evaluate the spatial transferability of the most stable model from this thesis (S2_only_diff SVM), the prototype was applied to an area near Lindau (Canton Zurich), entirely outside the airport training domain and temporally separated from the training period (2019-2023). Ground truth data consisting of four mowing event polygons dated 02.05.2025 were provided by Strickhof. Two Sentinel-2 scenes covering the area were manually downloaded from the Copernicus Browser (30.04.2025 as the before image, 10.05.2025 as the after image). The model was applied over the full scene extent without restricting the analysis to grassland areas, simulating a realistic use case where no prior land cover information is available. The resulting mowing predictions were compared to the ground truth polygons to assess the model’s generalisation performance in a new geographic context.

title: 3  Methods
text:
3.9 Use of Generative AI Tools
Generative AI tools were used as support during the development of this thesis. Claude (Anthropic, Claude Opus 4.6) was used for code development assistance, particularly for SAR data processing workflows with SNAP and Google Earth Engine, and for refining the language of the written report. Perplexity AI was used to support the initial identification of relevant scientific literature, with all sources subsequently verified and retrieved from primary databases. DeepL Translator and DeepL Write were used for translation between English and German and for language refinement. In all cases, the scientific content, methodological decisions, and interpretation of results are the author’s own work. All AI outputs were critically reviewed and verified before use. In particular, literature references identified through Perplexity AI required systematic verification, as initial suggestions frequently included misattributed or non-existent sources. title: 5  Discussion
text:
5.1 Optical Baseline and SAR Backscatter
The Sentinel-2-only models serve as the primary baseline for this thesis. Their test-set performance confirms the core finding of the preceding project work (Klaver 2025): pixel-based machine learning models using temporal differences in vegetation indices can detect mowing events with high accuracy when cloud-free imagery is available. The refined feature selection confirms that the mowing signal is concentrated in a small number of spectral change indicators. Reducing the feature set from five to three difference features produced a minimal drop in test-set F1-Score (0.923 to 0.920), but the scene-level evaluation suggests that the sparser _diff configurations generalise more reliably than the broader _best feature sets, consistent with the finding from the preceding study that fewer, structurally robust features outperform larger feature sets in operational application (Klaver 2025). This also aligns with the observation by Garioud et al. (2019) that simpler model configurations can be highly effective for mowing detection when training data is limited.
The GRD backscatter features showed negligible predictive value for mowing detection at this study site. The GRD-only configuration achieved near-random performance on the test set and failed completely at scene level (F1 around 0.200). Adding GRD features to the optical baseline did not improve performance at either level. An exception is scene 73, where the S2+GRD RF achieved the highest F1-Score (0.741), marginally above the S2-only_best RF (0.735). However, this advantage did not replicate on scene 12 or in the test-set evaluation, where including GRD features showed no systematic benefit. With only two evaluation scenes, such reversals are expected and do not override the broader pattern. The outcome is consistent with De Vroey et al. (2021), who reported that SAR backscatter alone is a weak predictor of mowing events due to confounding soil moisture, precipitation, and phenological variation. Reinermann et al. (2022) observed a similar pattern: their integrated S1+S2 approach reduced the F1-Score from 0.65 to 0.61 compared to the optical-only method, with the degradation attributed to increased false positives from SAR features. While backscatter changes after mowing are physically expected, particularly a decrease in VH due to the loss of canopy volume scattering (Meyer 2019), these changes appear to be small relative to the environmental noise floor at C-band frequencies and do not produce a reliable classification signal at the pixel level.

title: 5  Discussion
text:
5.2 Coherence Signal and Its Limitations
The integration of interferometric coherence was motivated by the expectation that mowed grassland, presenting a more stable scattering surface, would produce measurably higher coherence than tall, moving vegetation and with that a better, less noisy SAR signal compared to GRD. The seasonal coherence analysis (Section 4.1) shows that this expectation is only partially supported. A positive Cohen’s \(d\) was observed exclusively for VH polarisation during the late growing season. VV polarisation produced near-zero effect sizes across all seasons, and both polarisations showed negative Cohen’s \(d\) values during the early and peak seasons.
These results are weaker than what the reference literature reports. Tamm et al. (2016) found statistically significant coherence increases for both polarisations, whereas here only VH in the late season follows the expected pattern. De Vroey et al. (2021) achieved a 54% event detection rate from coherence jumps in hay meadows, substantially exceeding the coherence-based detection capability observed here, where coherence-only models achieved F1-Scores of 0.468 to 0.479 on test samples and approximately 0.200 at scene level.
Several factors likely contribute to this discrepancy. First, the airport grasslands are managed under specific operational protocols that differ from the agricultural grasslands studied by Tamm et al. (2016) and De Vroey et al. (2021), with potentially different grass species, cutting heights, and mowing frequencies. The absence of grazing, which De Vroey et al. identified as a major source of false detections, should theoretically improve coherence-based detection, yet performance remains poor. Second, the Sentinel-1 repeat cycle of 6 or 12 days means that rapid regrowth during the peak season can substantially reduce the coherence contrast before the second acquisition is recorded, aligning with Tamm et al.’s finding that the 12-day baseline proved insufficient during rapid growth phases.
The SNR correction following Tamm et al. (2016) consistently improved statistical separability by increasing Cohen’s \(d\) magnitudes and lowering p-values, but did not reverse the sign of the effect in any configuration, leaving the fundamental signal weakness unresolved.
These findings explain why coherence-only models achieved near-random F1-Scores in both training and operational application. While a coherence signal exists at the parcel level in late season, the per-pixel variability is too high for a pixel-based classifier to exploit reliably. A parcel-level or segment-based approach could potentially yield better class separability, but would sacrifice the ability to detect sub-parcel mowing patterns, a relevant use case at the airport where mowing frequently affects only portions of larger grassland areas.
Despite these limitations, including coherence features alongside optical features in the Full-fusion RF produced the highest test-set F1-Score within Group B (0.922) and competitive operational results, suggesting that the classifier can extract some complementary information from coherence even when the standalone signal is weak. The selective integration strategy, informed by permutation importance analysis, proved essential: adding all available features indiscriminately degraded performance for some classifiers, particularly the SVM.
An additional factor contributing to the weak pixel-level coherence signal is the resolution mismatch between the optical and SAR features. The coherence rasters were computed at 20 m and resampled to the 10 m optical grid using bilinear interpolation, meaning that each original coherence pixel covers four optical pixels. At parcel boundaries, where mowed and unmowed areas meet, this resampling produces blended coherence values that do not correspond to either class. For a pixel-based classifier operating at 10 m resolution, these mixed boundary pixels add noise to the coherence features without carrying discriminative information. This effect is difficult to separate from the inherent weakness of the C-band coherence signal at this site, but it likely contributes to the poor pixel-level class separability, particularly for smaller mowing events.

title: 5  Discussion
text:
5.3 Operational Improvements and Model Stability
The scene-level threshold calibration emerged as the single most impactful operational improvement. The calibrated thresholds for S2-based models ranged from 0.775 to 0.950, far above the default of 0.5, reflecting the severe class imbalance at scene level where typically less than 10% of grassland pixels are mowed at any given time. On scene 46, threshold calibration alone improved the F1-Score from 0.477 to 0.587, primarily by increasing precision while recall decreased moderately (Section 4.4). The calibrated thresholds for the coherence-only and GRD-only models (0.100 to 0.325) tell a different story. These near-minimum thresholds indicate that the optimal strategy for SAR-only models is to predict nearly every pixel as mowed, which simply maximises recall in the absence of a discriminative signal, effectively confirming that these features carry insufficient information for pixel-level mowing detection.
This improvement has direct implications for interpreting the postprocessing results. Spatial postprocessing methods such as morphological filtering target isolated false positive pixels (Blaschke 2010), the same noise that threshold calibration addresses at the decision level. Because the calibrated threshold already eliminates the majority of scattered false detections, the residual noise available for postprocessing is limited. This explains the marginal mean improvement of +0.005 F1 and the inconsistent effect across scenes (Section 4.5). In early experiments without threshold calibration, postprocessing produced substantially larger improvements, confirming that the two mechanisms target the same error source. Both operate on the same precision-recall axis: raising the threshold or applying morphological erosion reduces false positives at the cost of removing small true positive clusters. At this study site, false positives are the dominant error source, making aggressive noise reduction beneficial on average. However, for scenes where mowing events affect small or narrow areas, aggressive postprocessing can remove genuine detections, producing a net loss in F1. The poor performance of SLIC-based postprocessing (F1 dropping to approximately 0.239) illustrates a related limitation: because mowed and unmowed grass are spectrally similar, SLIC cannot delineate mowing boundaries, and during majority voting mowed pixels are outvoted by the surrounding unmowed majority within each segment. A joint optimisation of threshold and postprocessing parameters, rather than the sequential approach used here, could potentially yield better results but was beyond the scope of the current work.
Despite the overall improvements, no single model configuration performed consistently best across scenes. On scene 12, the S2-only_diff SVM achieved the highest F1-Score, while on scene 73, the S2-only_best RF performed best. This instability extends to the feature importance analysis, where rankings shifted substantially between Group A and Group B, most notably gndvi_diff, which showed negative importance in Group A but ranked among the top predictors in Group B. Because the two groups differ in both sample size and event composition (63 vs 24 events), this shift most likely reflects sensitivity to the specific training events included rather than a genuine change in the feature’s discriminative value. Scene-level evaluation amplifies this variability, as each scene represents a single snapshot with its own weather conditions, mowing patterns, and ground truth quality. A further source of uncertainty lies in the ground truth data itself: recorded by hand and subsequently digitised, spatial accuracy can be lost at both stages, and occasional inconsistencies suggest that some events may have been incompletely recorded. The control test on scene 46 supports this interpretation: when the model was applied to the non-event window (\(t_{n-2}\) to \(t_{n-1}\)), it produced virtually no false positive detections, while correctly identifying the majority of mowed pixels one time step later (Section 4.6). This contrast provides additional confidence that the model responds to genuine mowing-induced spectral changes rather than to background variation.
The enhanced workflow substantially improves upon the PW2 baseline, as shown in Section 4.6. On scene 73, the current most stable clearly surpasses the F1-Score (0.635 vs 0.397), while the improvement on scene 12 is smaller but consistent (0.674 vs 0.597). The improvement is driven primarily by precision, reflecting the combined effect of the multi-feature design and threshold calibration. Over all, the S2-only configurations offer the most consistent performance with the least data dependency, making them the most robust choice for operational deployment.
The generalisation test near Lindau provides further evidence that the workflow transfers beyond the training site. The model was applied to 2025 imagery on an unseen location, yet produced spatially coherent, parcel-shaped detections rather than scattered noise. Although the reported F1-Score of 0.511 is low, this is largely attributable to incomplete ground truth coverage, as visual comparison of the before and after RGB composites confirms that many areas flagged as false positives display spectral changes consistent with vegetation removal. The model did not produce false detections on forests, roads, buildings, or bare soil despite the absence of a grassland mask, suggesting that the spectral change features are sufficiently specific to grassland dynamics that a land cover mask is not required to prevent systematic misclassification of non-vegetated surfaces.

title: 5  Discussion
text:
5.4 Limitations
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the results of this study.
The ground truth data, recorded by hand and subsequently digitised, represent the single primary reference source. Despite substantial efforts to acquire additional ground truth from external institutions, no datasets with the required spatial and temporal resolution were obtained. The limited spatial precision of these records directly affects both model training and evaluation.
The models were trained and evaluated primarily on grasslands at Zurich Airport, which are managed under specific operational protocols that may not be representative of other grassland management contexts. The generalisation test near Lindau provides an encouraging but preliminary indication of spatial transferability: the reference data covers only four mowing polygons from a single provider on a single date, and mowing events on surrounding parcels are not documented, meaning the reported F1-Score likely represents a lower bound on actual performance. A robust assessment of transferability would require comprehensive ground truth across multiple sites and management regimes.
The coherence features were available for only 24 of the 63 training events due to strict temporal matching requirements and silent SNAP processing failures. The reduced sample size limits statistical power and means that comparisons between S2-only and S2+coherence models operate on different data subsets with different event compositions.
The coherence rasters were computed at 20 m resolution and resampled to 10 m to match the optical grid, introducing spatial smoothing. The mismatch in native resolution between optical and SAR features is a structural limitation of combining these sensor types.
The current coherence feature design uses only absolute coherence values from the pre-mowing and post-mowing pairs. Computing coherence temporal differences would require six SLC acquisitions per event, further reducing usable training events, and was therefore not pursued.
The NESZ values used for the SNR decorrelation correction (-25.0 dB for VV, -27.0 dB for VH) are fixed approximations that do not account for incidence-angle-dependent variation across the swath. While these values fall within the range of measured system performance, uncertainty in this parameter introduces a corresponding uncertainty in the corrected coherence values, particularly for low-backscatter pixels where the correction is largest.

title: 5  Discussion
text:
5.5 Conclusion and Outlook
This thesis investigated whether the integration of SAR interferometric coherence and spatial postprocessing methods can improve automated mowing detection from satellite imagery. The findings can be summarised with respect to the research questions posed in Chapter 1.
Regarding the integration of SAR data (Q1): GRD backscatter provided no useful signal for mowing detection. Interferometric coherence showed a physically meaningful but weak and season-dependent response on parcel-level that could not support standalone detection on pixel-level. When selectively combined with optical features, coherence tended to lower model performance on both balanced test-samples as well as operational scenarios. While SAR data is inherently cloud-independent, the weak discriminative power of both backscatter and coherence features at the pixel level means that SAR cannot serve as a standalone fallback when optical imagery is unavailable.
Regarding spatial postprocessing (Q2): morphological filtering and median pre-filtering produced small, inconsistent improvements in F1-Score. The limited impact is attributable to the effectiveness of threshold calibration, which addresses the same false positive noise. SLIC superpixel aggregation degraded performance at the tested parameter ranges.
Regarding ground truth acquisition (Q3): extensive efforts to obtain additional reference data were unsuccessful, confirming that the availability of spatially precise mowing records remains the primary bottleneck for scaling and validating mowing detection workflows.
Regarding the comparison with the PW2 baseline (Q4): the enhanced workflow substantially improves upon the baseline, greatly increasing the operational F1-Score on one evaluation scene. The improvement is driven by the multi-feature design and threshold calibration rather than by SAR data. The control test confirmed that the model responds to genuine mowing signals rather than unrelated spectral variation. Based on overall stability across evaluation scenes and the generalisation test, the S2-only_diff SVM with LOO-calibrated threshold and minimal postprocessing is recommended as the most operationally robust configuration. It requires only three input features, avoids dependence on post-event absolute reflectance values that may vary across sites, and demonstrated consistent performance on both airport scenes and the independent Lindau test area.
For future work, the most impactful direction would be acquiring diverse, spatially precise ground truth data across multiple sites and management regimes to enable robust validation and transferability assessment. For coherence, a parcel-level classification approach where coherence is spatially averaged before classification could yield better results than the pixel-based approach pursued here. Computing coherence temporal differences from six-acquisition sequences could provide stronger features, if sufficient SLC data availability can be ensured. Evaluating the operational workflow systematically across a broader range of locations and years would provide the statistical basis needed to identify a reliably optimal model configuration and to assess long-term stability under varying phenological and atmospheric conditions.

title: Statement of Reproducibility
text:
Statement of Reproducibility



All code developed for data processing, model training, evaluation, and the operational prototype is fully available in the project’s GitHub repository. The ground truth data provided by Zurich Airport is confidential and cannot be publicly shared, but the code structure allows reproduction of the workflow using similar datasets. Sentinel-2 imagery is openly available through the Copernicus Browser. Sentinel-1 GRD data were accessed via Google Earth Engine, and SLC products were acquired from the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem using the cdsetool library. Both sources are publicly accessible, though both acquisitions require user credentials that are not included in the repository. The official land survey and fire brigade responsibility area data are openly available from the Canton of Zurich geoportal.
To ensure reproducibility and maintainability, set random seeds were used throughout all model training and splitting procedures. The codebase was organised into documented, modular functions in a dedicated src directory, preventing code duplication and allowing individual pipeline steps to be reused independently. Key configuration variables and parameters (e.g., temporal window sizes, cloud probability thresholds, feature sets, postprocessing parameters) are declared at the top of each notebook to facilitate adaptation. The standalone prototype notebook for operational mowing detection is fully self-contained and does not depend on the project’s source modules. Project version control was managed via GitHub. All computational tasks, including SAR coherence processing via SNAP GPT, were run on standard local hardware.
